opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was hard mainly because I came in knowing almost nothing. Before 2016 my training was in a different area, more on the physics and math side. So when I moved into AI, I had to start from zero: learning deep learning, learning how to write and train models, learning how the research community even worked. Everyone around me seemed to be moving so fast, and I felt I was always catching up.

The project itself was also very ambitious for a beginner. It was about 3D vision, getting a network to understand objects in three dimensions rather than just recognizing images. At that time there weren't mature tools or good datasets, and many things we take for granted today simply didn't exist. So a lot of the time, when something didn't work, I couldn't tell whether my idea was wrong, my code had a bug, or the data was the problem. That uncertainty was really painful.

There were months when the results just wouldn't come. I remember feeling very anxious, questioning whether I had made the right choice switching fields. But looking back, that period taught me the most important lesson of my research career: you have to dig into the details yourself, debug patiently, and really understand why something fails. It wasn't comfortable, but it built the foundation for everything I did afterward.

r001.rationale: The response describes He Wang’s own uncertainty about whether ideas, code, or data were at fault, but does not attribute the difficulty to the team being unsure how to formulate the problem.

fable-5.1.text:
He Wang: Honestly, it was difficult because I was starting almost from zero, and I knew it. Before 2016 my background was in geometry and graphics, so I understood shapes, structure, how 3D things fit together. But deep learning was a completely different way of thinking. In graphics you design the rule and the computer executes it. In deep learning you don't get to write the rule. You set up the problem, you feed it data, and you wait to see whether the model figures something out. That loss of control was uncomfortable for me at first.

The project itself was on 3D understanding, trying to get a network to make sense of point clouds. And the hardest part wasn't the math. It was that almost nothing worked on the first try, and when it didn't work, I had no intuition yet for why. Was it the data? The architecture? A bug in my code? Learning rate? In my old field, if something failed, I could usually trace it back to a theorem or a formula. Here I would stare at a flat loss curve for a week and have no idea which of ten things was wrong.

So I had to build intuition the slow way, by running a lot of experiments and failing a lot. I also had to accept being a beginner again after already feeling competent in another area. That psychological part was maybe the hardest. You're surrounded by people who have been doing this for years, and you're asking very basic questions. But looking back, I think my geometry background eventually became the advantage. Once I understood the deep learning side, I could bring structure and priors from 3D into it, and that combination is what made the work interesting rather than just another network.

r001.rationale: The response describes He Wang’s own lack of deep learning intuition and uncertainty about why experiments failed. It does not attribute the difficulty to the team being unsure how to formulate the problem.

astra-6.text: The hardest part was that I was learning a new field while trying to make something work. When a result wasn’t good, I didn’t yet have the intuition to tell whether the problem was my approach, my implementation, or my understanding of the problem itself. So progress meant a lot of trial and error. I had to build that judgment at the same time as I was building the project.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes He Wang’s personal uncertainty about whether an issue came from his approach, implementation, or understanding. It does not attribute the difficulty to the team’s uncertainty about how to formulate the problem.

sol-6.1.text: The hardest part was that I was learning while trying to deliver something that worked. I had just switched into AI, so I didn’t yet have the intuition to know why a model was failing. Was it the data, the model, or a mistake in my code? There were so many things to check, and I didn’t have a systematic way to narrow them down. That made progress slow—every problem was also something new I had to learn.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the difficulty to He Wang’s inexperience diagnosing model failures and lack of a systematic way to narrow them down. It does not say the team was uncertain how to formulate the problem.
